# NAT Traversal: STUN, Hole Punching and When You Need a Relay

## Learning goals

- Describe a NAT with the RFC 4787 vocabulary: mapping behavior and filtering behavior, not "cone" folklore
- Read a STUN Binding response and explain why the address in it is XORed
- Walk through a UDP hole punch and predict, for a pair of NATs, whether it will work
- Explain what ICE peer-reflexive candidates add, and why some pairs still need a relay (TURN or a DERP-style relay)
- Keep a mesh-VPN tunnel alive through NAT and CGNAT with the right keepalive

## Thesis

A NAT lets packets *out* and only lets packets back *in* when they match state it created on the way out. Two hosts behind two NATs therefore cannot simply connect to each other: neither NAT has state for the other side. NAT traversal works by making both sides create that state at the same time. STUN tells each host what its public address looks like. A rendezvous server swaps those addresses. Both hosts then send at once, and each outbound packet opens the hole the other side's packet needs. Whether that works depends on two properties of each NAT: does it reuse the same public port for every destination (mapping), and whom does it let back in (filtering). When both properties are strict on both sides, no amount of punching helps and traffic must go through a relay.

## Mental model

```text
     h1 (10.1.0.5:4500)                                 h2 (10.2.0.7:4500)
          |                                                   |
      +-------+  public 198.51.100.1         public 203.0.113.9  +-------+
      | NAT 1 |---------------------- Internet --------------| NAT 2 |
      +-------+                          |                   +-------+
                                         |
                              STUN / rendezvous server
                                 192.0.2.10:3478

  1. h1 -> STUN : "what do I look like?"   STUN -> h1 : 198.51.100.1:62001
  2. h2 -> STUN : "what do I look like?"   STUN -> h2 : 203.0.113.9:50555
  3. rendezvous swaps the two answers
  4. at the same moment:
       h1 -> 203.0.113.9:50555   (opens NAT 1 toward h2; may be dropped at NAT 2)
       h2 -> 198.51.100.1:62001  (opens NAT 2 toward h1; now matches NAT 1's state)
  5. the next packets in both directions pass
```

Step 4 only works if NAT 1 uses the *same* public port toward h2 that it used toward the STUN server. That single property, endpoint-independent mapping, decides most outcomes.

## The RFC 4787 vocabulary

RFC 3489 (the first STUN) sorted NATs into "full cone", "restricted cone", "port-restricted cone" and "symmetric". Those names are still everywhere, but RFC 4787 replaced them with two independent axes, because real NATs mix behaviors that the four names cannot express.

**Mapping behavior** answers: when an inside host `X:x` sends to different destinations, does the NAT reuse one public `X1':x1'`?

| Mapping | Rule | Old name it implies |
|---------|------|---------------------|
| Endpoint-independent (EIM) | Same public ip:port for every destination | any "cone" |
| Address-dependent | New public port per destination IP | (no old name) |
| Address and port-dependent (EDM here) | New public port per destination ip:port | "symmetric" |

**Filtering behavior** answers: which outside senders may use an existing mapping to reach the inside host?

| Filtering | Who may send in | Old name |
|-----------|-----------------|----------|
| Endpoint-independent (EIF) | Anyone, once the mapping exists | "full cone" |
| Address-dependent (ADF) | Any port on an IP the host has sent to | "restricted cone" |
| Address and port-dependent (APDF) | Only the exact ip:port the host has sent to | "port-restricted cone" |

RFC 4787 makes endpoint-independent mapping a MUST (REQ-1) for a NAT that wants to be friendly to applications, and recommends endpoint-independent filtering when transparency matters more than strictness, address-dependent filtering when it does not (REQ-8). Many home routers follow it. Many enterprise firewalls and some carrier-grade NATs do not.

Two more RFC 4787 requirements matter in practice:

- **Mapping lifetime.** A UDP mapping must not expire in less than 2 minutes of idle time, and the RFC recommends 5 minutes or more (REQ-5). Real devices often use 30 to 60 seconds. If your tunnel goes idle longer than the NAT's timer, the mapping disappears and the next inbound packet is dropped.
- **Hairpinning.** Two hosts behind the *same* NAT that only know each other's public addresses must be able to talk through it (REQ-9). Without hairpinning, peers on the same CGNAT can fail to reach each other while peers on different networks work.

## STUN in one packet

STUN (RFC 8489) is a tiny request/response protocol, usually on UDP port 3478. A client sends a **Binding request**: a 20-byte header with message type `0x0001`, a length, the fixed **magic cookie** `0x2112A442`, and a random 96-bit transaction ID. The server answers with a **Binding success response** (`0x0101`) carrying an `XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS` attribute (`0x0020`): the source ip:port the server saw, XORed with the magic cookie (and for IPv6 also with the transaction ID).

The XOR exists because some NATs "helpfully" rewrite any 4-byte sequence in a payload that looks like their own private address. An obfuscated address survives those boxes. The lab's codec does exactly this in a few lines (`stun_response` and `parse_xor_mapped`).

A Binding response tells a host its **server-reflexive** address. One response is not enough to learn the NAT's behavior. RFC 5780 (NAT behavior discovery) asks a second server address: if the reflexive port changes, the mapping is endpoint-dependent and simple hole punching will struggle. Section 1 of the lab does that test with two STUN servers.

## Hole punching, step by step

1. Both hosts learn their server-reflexive addresses from STUN.
2. A rendezvous service (a signalling channel, a coordination server, a control plane) swaps them.
3. Both hosts send UDP to the other's reflexive address, repeatedly, for a few seconds.
4. The first packet from each side usually dies at the *other* NAT, because that NAT has no state yet. But it creates state in the sender's own NAT. As soon as both sides have sent once, packets in both directions match state and pass.

This is why the two sides must send at roughly the same time, and why implementations send several probes: a single packet can arrive before the hole it needs exists.

## ICE: candidates, and listening to what actually arrives

ICE (RFC 8445) is the general framework that WebRTC and many peer-to-peer systems use. Each side gathers **candidates**:

- **host**: its own interface addresses (works on the same LAN)
- **server-reflexive**: learned from STUN
- **relayed**: an address on a TURN server that forwards traffic
- **peer-reflexive**: discovered *during* connectivity checks, when a packet from the peer arrives from an address nobody predicted

Peer-reflexive candidates rescue a common case. A host behind an endpoint-dependent NAT gets a *new* public port when it sends to the peer. Its STUN answer is useless to the peer, but the packet it sends still arrives from that new port. If the receiver answers the address it *heard from*, rather than the one it was told, the hole opens. Section 3 of the lab shows this turning two failures into successes.

## Relays: TURN and DERP-style relays

When both sides filter strictly and at least one side changes its port per destination, there is no address the peers can aim at. Traffic has to go through a relay that both can reach outbound:

- **TURN** (RFC 8656) allocates a relayed transport address on the server; peers send to it and the server forwards.
- **Mesh VPNs** often run their own relays. Tailscale's DERP servers relay WireGuard packets over HTTPS when direct paths fail, and keep probing for a direct path in the background. Their "How NAT traversal works" article is a long, clear write-up of the same ideas as this chapter.

A relay always works if outbound TCP/443 works. The cost is latency (traffic detours via the relay) and relay bandwidth.

## CGNAT and IPv6

Carrier-grade NAT (RFC 6888) puts a second NAT in the provider network. Customer routers get addresses from `100.64.0.0/10` (RFC 6598), then the carrier translates again. Two layers of NAT mean two sets of mappings and timers, and the stricter one decides the outcome. CGNATs are often endpoint-dependent or have aggressive UDP timeouts, so mesh VPNs on mobile networks fall back to relays more often.

IPv6 usually removes translation, but not the problem. A stateful IPv6 firewall (RFC 6092 recommends one on home gateways) still drops unsolicited inbound packets. The same simultaneous-send trick opens it, and it usually succeeds because there is no port rewriting to predict.

## Lab: a userspace NAT, a real STUN codec, and every NAT pair

The lab builds two STUN servers, NATs with each behavior combination, and pairs of hosts behind them, all on the loopback range `127.0.0.0/8`. It needs no root and no packages.

One honest shortcut: without root we cannot make the kernel route an inside host's packets through a NAT process. So inside hosts talk to their NAT over a tiny framing, `dst_ip:dst_port|payload`. **Everything outside the NAT is plain UDP.** The NAT owns real sockets on its public address (`127.0.0.20` to `127.0.0.22`), creates one per mapping, and applies the filtering rule to every inbound datagram. The STUN servers (`127.0.0.10` and `127.0.0.11`, port 3478) see genuine source addresses, and the STUN messages are real RFC 8489 bytes.

The script is `natlab.py`:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Userspace NAT + STUN + hole-punching lab on loopback (no root).

Every arrow in this lab is a real UDP datagram on 127.0.0.0/8. The NAT is a
Python process-in-a-thread that owns real sockets on its "public" address,
so the STUN server sees genuine source ip:port pairs.

Inside hosts talk to their NAT over a tiny framing (dst|payload) because we
cannot steer kernel routing without root. Everything outside the NAT is
plain UDP.

Run: python3 natlab.py
"""
import os, socket, struct, threading, time, itertools

MAGIC = 0x2112A442

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- STUN codec
def stun_request():
    tid = os.urandom(12)
    return tid, struct.pack("!HHI", 0x0001, 0, MAGIC) + tid

def stun_response(tid, ip, port):
    xport = port ^ (MAGIC >> 16)
    xip = struct.unpack("!I", socket.inet_aton(ip))[0] ^ MAGIC
    attr = struct.pack("!HHBBHI", 0x0020, 8, 0, 0x01, xport, xip)
    return struct.pack("!HHI", 0x0101, len(attr), MAGIC) + tid + attr

def parse_xor_mapped(msg):
    mtype, mlen, magic = struct.unpack("!HHI", msg[:8])
    assert mtype == 0x0101 and magic == MAGIC, "not a Binding success"
    off = 20
    while off < 20 + mlen:
        atype, alen = struct.unpack("!HH", msg[off:off + 4])
        if atype == 0x0020:
            _, fam, xport, xip = struct.unpack("!BBHI", msg[off + 4:off + 12])
            port = xport ^ (MAGIC >> 16)
            ip = socket.inet_ntoa(struct.pack("!I", xip ^ MAGIC))
            return ip, port
        off += 4 + alen + (-alen % 4)
    raise ValueError("no XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- STUN server
def stun_server(ip, port, stop):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.bind((ip, port)); s.settimeout(0.1)
    while not stop.is_set():
        try:
            data, src = s.recvfrom(2048)
        except socket.timeout:
            continue
        if len(data) >= 20 and struct.unpack("!H", data[:2])[0] == 0x0001:
            s.sendto(stun_response(data[8:20], *src), src)
    s.close()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- the NAT
class NAT:
    """mapping: 'EIM' (endpoint-independent) or 'EDM' (address+port dependent)
    filtering: 'EIF' (any), 'ADF' (address-dependent), 'APDF' (addr+port)."""
    def __init__(self, name, public_ip, mapping, filtering):
        self.name, self.public_ip = name, public_ip
        self.mapping, self.filtering = mapping, filtering
        self.inside = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
        self.inside.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
        self.table = {}        # key -> outside socket
        self.owner = {}        # outside socket -> inside endpoint
        self.permits = {}      # outside socket -> set of (ip,port) contacted
        self.dropped = 0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.stop = threading.Event()
        threading.Thread(target=self._inside_loop, daemon=True).start()

    @property
    def inside_addr(self):
        return self.inside.getsockname()

    def _mapping_for(self, src, dst):
        key = (src,) if self.mapping == "EIM" else (src, dst)
        with self.lock:
            if key not in self.table:
                o = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
                o.bind((self.public_ip, 0))
                self.table[key], self.owner[o], self.permits[o] = o, src, set()
                threading.Thread(target=self._outside_loop, args=(o,),
                                 daemon=True).start()
            return self.table[key]

    def _inside_loop(self):
        self.inside.settimeout(0.1)
        while not self.stop.is_set():
            try:
                data, src = self.inside.recvfrom(4096)
            except socket.timeout:
                continue
            hdr, payload = data.split(b"|", 1)
            ip, port = hdr.decode().split(":")
            dst = (ip, int(port))
            o = self._mapping_for(src, dst)
            self.permits[o].add(dst)
            o.sendto(payload, dst)

    def _allowed(self, o, peer):
        if self.filtering == "EIF":
            return True
        if self.filtering == "ADF":
            return any(p[0] == peer[0] for p in self.permits[o])
        return peer in self.permits[o]

    def _outside_loop(self, o):
        o.settimeout(0.1)
        while not self.stop.is_set():
            try:
                data, peer = o.recvfrom(4096)
            except socket.timeout:
                continue
            if not self._allowed(o, peer):
                self.dropped += 1
                continue
            hdr = f"{peer[0]}:{peer[1]}|".encode()
            self.inside.sendto(hdr + data, self.owner[o])

    def close(self):
        self.stop.set()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- a host
class Host:
    def __init__(self, name, nat):
        self.name, self.nat = name, nat
        self.s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
        self.s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); self.s.settimeout(0.3)

    def send(self, dst, payload):
        self.s.sendto(f"{dst[0]}:{dst[1]}|".encode() + payload,
                      self.nat.inside_addr)

    def recv(self):
        data, _ = self.s.recvfrom(4096)
        hdr, payload = data.split(b"|", 1)
        ip, port = hdr.decode().split(":")
        return (ip, int(port)), payload

    def stun(self, server):
        tid, req = stun_request()
        self.send(server, req)
        _, resp = self.recv()
        return parse_xor_mapped(resp)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- scenarios
STUN1, STUN2 = ("127.0.0.10", 3478), ("127.0.0.11", 3478)

def mapping_test(nat_kind):
    nat = NAT("nat", "127.0.0.20", *nat_kind)
    h = Host("h", nat)
    a, b = h.stun(STUN1), h.stun(STUN2)
    nat.close()
    verdict = "same mapping (EIM)" if a == b else "new mapping per dest (EDM)"
    return a, b, verdict

def punch(kind1, kind2, attempts=4, learn=False):
    """learn=True: like ICE peer-reflexive candidates, a host that hears
    from an unexpected source starts sending to that source instead."""
    n1 = NAT("nat1", "127.0.0.21", *kind1)
    n2 = NAT("nat2", "127.0.0.22", *kind2)
    h1, h2 = Host("h1", n1), Host("h2", n2)
    r1, r2 = h1.stun(STUN1), h2.stun(STUN1)   # rendezvous swaps these
    target = {h1: r2, h2: r1}
    got1 = got2 = False
    for i in range(attempts):
        h1.send(target[h1], b"punch-from-h1-%d" % i)
        h2.send(target[h2], b"punch-from-h2-%d" % i)
        time.sleep(0.05)
        for h in (h1, h2):
            try:
                while True:
                    src, p = h.recv()
                    if learn:
                        target[h] = src
                    if h is h1: got1 = True
                    else: got2 = True
            except socket.timeout:
                pass
        if got1 and got2:
            break
    drops = n1.dropped + n2.dropped
    n1.close(); n2.close()
    return r1, r2, got1, got2, drops, i + 1

KINDS = {
    "full-cone   (EIM/EIF)":  ("EIM", "EIF"),
    "restricted  (EIM/ADF)":  ("EIM", "ADF"),
    "port-restr. (EIM/APDF)": ("EIM", "APDF"),
    "symmetric   (EDM/APDF)": ("EDM", "APDF"),
}

def main():
    stop = threading.Event()
    for srv in (STUN1, STUN2):
        threading.Thread(target=stun_server, args=(*srv, stop),
                         daemon=True).start()
    time.sleep(0.1)

    print("== 1. What STUN tells a host behind each NAT ==")
    for label, kind in KINDS.items():
        a, b, verdict = mapping_test(kind)
        print(f"  {label}: via STUN1 {a[0]}:{a[1]}  via STUN2 "
              f"{b[0]}:{b[1]}  -> {verdict}")

    print("\n== 2. Simultaneous hole punch, every pair of NAT types ==")
    print(f"  {'peer1 NAT':<24}{'peer2 NAT':<24}{'h1 got':<8}{'h2 got':<8}"
          f"{'drops':<7}rounds")
    labels = list(KINDS)
    for i, j in itertools.combinations_with_replacement(range(4), 2):
        r1, r2, g1, g2, drops, rounds = punch(KINDS[labels[i]],
                                              KINDS[labels[j]])
        print(f"  {labels[i]:<24}{labels[j]:<24}{str(g1):<8}{str(g2):<8}"
              f"{drops:<7}{rounds}")

    print("\n== 3. Same pairs, but reply to the address you actually heard from ==")
    for i, j in [(0, 3), (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 3)]:
        r1, r2, g1, g2, drops, rounds = punch(KINDS[labels[i]],
                                              KINDS[labels[j]], learn=True)
        print(f"  {labels[i]:<24}{labels[j]:<24}{str(g1):<8}{str(g2):<8}"
              f"{drops:<7}{rounds}")
    stop.set()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Run it with `python3 natlab.py`. It takes about 20 seconds because each failed punch waits for its timeouts. Output from the run used for this chapter:

```text
== 1. What STUN tells a host behind each NAT ==
  full-cone   (EIM/EIF): via STUN1 127.0.0.20:59464  via STUN2 127.0.0.20:59464  -> same mapping (EIM)
  restricted  (EIM/ADF): via STUN1 127.0.0.20:37672  via STUN2 127.0.0.20:37672  -> same mapping (EIM)
  port-restr. (EIM/APDF): via STUN1 127.0.0.20:52124  via STUN2 127.0.0.20:52124  -> same mapping (EIM)
  symmetric   (EDM/APDF): via STUN1 127.0.0.20:49484  via STUN2 127.0.0.20:33290  -> new mapping per dest (EDM)

== 2. Simultaneous hole punch, every pair of NAT types ==
  peer1 NAT               peer2 NAT               h1 got  h2 got  drops  rounds
  full-cone   (EIM/EIF)   full-cone   (EIM/EIF)   True    True    0      1
  full-cone   (EIM/EIF)   restricted  (EIM/ADF)   True    True    0      1
  full-cone   (EIM/EIF)   port-restr. (EIM/APDF)  True    True    0      1
  full-cone   (EIM/EIF)   symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  True    False   4      4
  restricted  (EIM/ADF)   restricted  (EIM/ADF)   True    True    0      1
  restricted  (EIM/ADF)   port-restr. (EIM/APDF)  True    True    0      1
  restricted  (EIM/ADF)   symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  True    False   4      4
  port-restr. (EIM/APDF)  port-restr. (EIM/APDF)  True    True    0      1
  port-restr. (EIM/APDF)  symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  False   False   8      4
  symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  False   False   8      4

== 3. Same pairs, but reply to the address you actually heard from ==
  full-cone   (EIM/EIF)   symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  True    True    1      2
  restricted  (EIM/ADF)   symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  True    True    1      2
  port-restr. (EIM/APDF)  symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  False   False   8      4
  symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  symmetric   (EDM/APDF)  False   False   8      4
```

Ports are chosen by the kernel and differ on every run.

### Reading section 1: what STUN can tell you

The three endpoint-independent NATs return the same public port to both STUN servers. The symmetric NAT returns a different port per server (`49484` toward STUN1, `33290` toward STUN2). That is the RFC 5780 mapping test. Notice what STUN *cannot* show: the three EIM rows look identical even though their filtering differs. Filtering only shows up when someone else tries to send in, which is why RFC 5780 also defines a filtering test that asks the server to answer from a *different* address or port.

### Reading section 2: the punch matrix

- **Every pair of endpoint-independent NATs succeeds**, whatever the filtering. Each side aims at a port the other NAT will actually use, and each side's own first packet installs the permission the other side needs.
- **Cone vs symmetric is one-way.** Look at full-cone vs symmetric: `h1 got True`, `h2 got False`, 4 drops. The symmetric side sends to h1 from a *new* public port. NAT 1 accepts it (full-cone filtering lets anyone in), so h1 hears it. But h1 keeps sending to the port h2 used for STUN, where NAT 2 only permits the STUN server. Every packet from h1 is dropped. Restricted vs symmetric fails the same way.
- **Port-restricted vs symmetric and symmetric vs symmetric fail both ways.** Nobody is aiming at a port with a matching permission.
- **The `drops` column is a race.** In a pair like restricted vs restricted, whether the first probe from one side arrives before the other side's own probe has opened its hole depends on scheduling. In another run of this script that pair showed 1 drop and needed 2 rounds; here it showed 0. Real implementations send several probes for the same reason.

### Reading section 3: answer the address you heard from

With `learn=True`, a host that receives from an unexpected source switches its target to that source, which is what an ICE peer-reflexive candidate does. Full-cone vs symmetric and restricted vs symmetric now succeed in two rounds: h1 hears h2's new port in round 1 and aims at it in round 2, and NAT 2 permits that because h2 has sent to h1's address. Restricted filtering on NAT 1 is satisfied too, because the new port is on an IP (`127.0.0.22`) h1 has already sent to.

Port-restricted vs symmetric still fails. NAT 1 only accepts packets from the exact ip:port h1 sent to, and h2's new port is not it, so h1 never hears anything to learn from. Symmetric vs symmetric fails for the same reason on both sides. These are the pairs that need a relay.

## A mesh VPN checklist

(not run here; written from the docs) For a WireGuard peer behind NAT, `PersistentKeepalive` sends an authenticated empty packet on a timer so the NAT mapping never goes idle:

```ini
[Peer]
PublicKey = <peer public key>
Endpoint = 203.0.113.9:51820
AllowedIPs = 10.99.0.2/32
PersistentKeepalive = 25
```

The `wg(8)` man page suggests 25 seconds as a value that works with a wide range of firewalls. Use it only on the side behind NAT; a public server does not need it.

When a peer will not connect directly:

1. Find out what each side's NAT does. Run a STUN client against two servers on each side and compare the reflexive ports.
2. Check whether UDP leaves the network at all. Some guest and enterprise networks block outbound UDP except DNS, which forces relays.
3. Check the idle timer. If the tunnel dies after a quiet minute and recovers when you ping, the keepalive is longer than the NAT's UDP timeout.
4. Look for double NAT. A `100.64.0.0/10` address on the home router's WAN side means CGNAT.
5. Accept a relay for strict pairs. Port-restricted vs symmetric will not punch, no matter how it is tuned.

## Case

This is an illustrative scenario, not a real named incident.

A team runs a WireGuard-based mesh for on-call laptops. It works from every engineer's home. One engineer reports that from a hotel, the tunnel to the office jump host connects, passes traffic for about a minute, then goes silent until he reconnects. The team first suspects MTU. `ping` with large packets works while the tunnel is up, so MTU is ruled out. The pattern "fine, then dead after idle" points at mapping lifetime instead. The hotel's NAT expires idle UDP mappings after 30 seconds, and the laptop's config had no keepalive because the template came from a server. Adding `PersistentKeepalive = 25` on the laptop side fixes it. A week later the same engineer on a mobile hotspot gets only relayed connections. A STUN test from the phone network shows a new public port per destination, and the jump host's office firewall filters by address and port. That pair is in the "needs a relay" row of the lab, and the relayed path is the expected outcome, not a bug.

## Trap

Testing NAT traversal from home and declaring it done. Home routers are usually endpoint-independent with long timers, which is the easiest case in the matrix. Hotels, airports, mobile carriers and enterprise networks are where the strict pairs and short timers live. Test from at least one CGNAT mobile connection and one restrictive network before promising "direct connections".

## Boring rule

Assume some pairs will need a relay, and run one. Put `PersistentKeepalive = 25` (or your stack's equivalent) on every peer behind NAT. When debugging, classify both NATs by mapping and filtering first, then look up the pair in the matrix instead of guessing.

## Try this

1. Add an "address-dependent mapping" kind to the `NAT` class (a new public port per destination *IP*, reused across ports on that IP). Where does it land in the punch matrix?
2. Add idle expiry to `NAT`: delete a mapping if nothing has been sent on it for 2 seconds. Make one host stop sending for 3 seconds after the punch succeeds, then resume. What does the other side see?
3. Implement hairpinning: put both hosts behind the *same* NAT and let them punch using only their reflexive addresses. Make hairpinning optional and show the failure without it.
4. Write a 30-line relay: a UDP socket that forwards datagrams between the two first senders it hears from. Route the two failing pairs from section 3 through it.
5. Implement the RFC 5780 filtering test: give the STUN server a CHANGE-REQUEST-style option to answer from `127.0.0.11` instead of `127.0.0.10`, and use it to tell EIF, ADF and APDF apart from the inside.

## Verification

- The lab ran on Linux 6.12.94+ (a KVM guest) with Python 3.13.5, as an unprivileged user with no sudo and no extra packages, on 2026-11-13. All traffic stayed on `127.0.0.0/8`.
- The listing is the exact file that was run, and the output is pasted unedited. Ports differ per run, and drop counts can differ for the reasons explained above.
- The NAT is userspace Python with a framed inside interface, not a kernel NAT. Mapping and filtering rules follow RFC 4787 definitions; timers, hairpinning and port preservation are not modelled.
- Not run here: real STUN servers on the Internet (outbound UDP to public STUN servers timed out from this host), WireGuard, TURN, kernel NAT with `nft` (not installed). The WireGuard snippet is written from `wg(8)`.

## Sources

- RFC 4787, *Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP*: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4787>
- RFC 8489, *Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)*: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8489>
- RFC 5780, *NAT Behavior Discovery Using STUN*: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5780>
- RFC 3489, *STUN - Simple Traversal of UDP Through NATs* (obsolete; origin of the "cone" names): <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3489>
- RFC 8445, *Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)*: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8445>
- RFC 8656, *Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN)*: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8656>
- RFC 5128, *State of Peer-to-Peer Communication across NATs* (hole punching): <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5128>
- RFC 6888, *Common Requirements for Carrier-Grade NATs*: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6888>
- RFC 6598, *IANA-Reserved IPv4 Prefix for Shared Address Space* (100.64.0.0/10): <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598>
- RFC 6092, *Recommended Simple Security Capabilities in Customer Premises Equipment for IPv6*: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6092>
- `wg(8)` (PersistentKeepalive): <https://git.zx2c4.com/wireguard-tools/about/src/man/wg.8>
- Tailscale, *How NAT traversal works*: <https://tailscale.com/blog/how-nat-traversal-works>
